statement.p: Suppose g is a function which has continuous derivatives, and that g(7)=4, g'(7)=1, g''(7)=5, g'''(7)=-4.
(a) What is the Taylor polynomial of degree 2 for g near 7?
(b) What is the Taylor polynomial of degree 3 for g near 7?
(c) Use the two polynomials that you found in parts (a) and (b) to approximate g(6.9).

static.solution:
g(x) = g(7) + g'(7)(x-7) + \frac{g''(7)}{2!}(x-7)^2 +\frac{g'''(7)}{3!}(x-7)^3+\cdots Substituting gives g(x) = 4 + 1(x-7) + \frac{5}{2!}(x-7)^2 +\frac{-4}{3!}(x-7)^3+\cdots
(a) The degree 2 Taylor polynomial, T_2 (x), is obtained by truncating after the (x-7)^2 term: T_2(x) = 4+1\mathopen{}\left(x-7\right)+\frac{1}{2!}\cdot 5\mathopen{}\left(x-7\right)^{2}.
(b) The degree 3 Taylor polynomial, T_3 (x), is obtained by truncating after the (x-7)^3 term: T_3 (x) = 4+1\mathopen{}\left(x-7\right)+\frac{1}{2!}\cdot 5\mathopen{}\left(x-7\right)^{2}+\frac{1}{3!}\mathopen{}\left(-4\right)\mathopen{}\left(x-7\right)^{3}
(c) Substitute x=6.9 into the Taylor polynomial of degree 2: T_2(4.9) = 4+1\mathopen{}\left(6.9-7\right)+\frac{1}{2!}\cdot 5\mathopen{}\left(6.9-7\right)^{2} = 3.925. From the Taylor polynomial of degree 3, we obtain T_3(4.9) = 4+1\mathopen{}\left(6.9-7\right)+\frac{1}{2!}\cdot 5\mathopen{}\left(6.9-7\right)^{2}+\frac{1}{3!}\mathopen{}\left(-4\right)\mathopen{}\left(6.9-7\right)^{3} = 3.92567.
